chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hasan, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr ibn Abi al-Sammal al-Asadi, from the one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
The dying person has more right over his wealth for as long as the soul remains within him.

key_terms.أَوْلَى: More rightful/having priority — a legal term indicating precedence in rights
key_terms.الرُّوحُ: The soul/spirit — its presence marks the boundary of legal life and ownership rights
key_terms.الْمَيِّتُ: The dying/near-death person — used here not for someone already dead, but one at the point of death (in articulo mortis)

ai.seo_question: Does a dying person retain rights over their wealth before death in Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a fundamental legal principle in Islamic inheritance law: a person retains full rights over their property as long as they are alive, even if they are on their deathbed. The hadith addresses disputes that may arise when heirs anticipate an inheritance — the dying person's wishes and gifts remain legally valid and take precedence. In the early Islamic legal context, this ruling was significant because it clarified that death-bed gifts and bequests (unlike posthumous distributions) are at the full discretion of the dying person, up until the moment of death.

en.hubeali:
Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Ali Bin Al Hassan, from Ibrahim Bin Abu Bakr Bin Abu Al Sammal Al Asady, from the one who informed him, 
Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> has said:
‘The dying one is higher with (the distribution of his wealth) for as long as there is the soul within him’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ahmad ibn Muhammad has narrated from Ali ibn al-Hassan from Ibrahim ibn abu Bakr al-Samal al-Asadiy from those who narrated to him who has narrated the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘
One who is about to die is more rightful to his assets as long as he is alive.’”
